opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed quite a bit. Early on, a lot of us assumed the right form factor was basically autocomplete on steroids: the model sits in your editor, watches you type, and suggests the next few lines. That was useful, but it kept the human in the driver's seat for every keystroke, and it didn't really use what the models were becoming capable of.

As the models got better at reasoning and at working over longer horizons, we realized the more interesting shape was something closer to a teammate you delegate to. You hand it a task, like "fix this bug," "add this feature," or "write tests for this module," and it goes off, explores the codebase, runs things, iterates, and comes back with a result you can review. That's a very different interaction. It's less about speed per keystroke and more about how much meaningful work you can offload while you focus on something else.

What I've come to believe is that there isn't one form factor. There's a spectrum. Sometimes you want the agent right there with you in the terminal or IDE, pairing in tight loops, where you can steer it every few seconds. Other times you want to fire off five tasks in parallel to a cloud environment and check back in an hour. The real challenge is making those feel like the same agent, with the same context and the same understanding of your codebase and preferences, so you can move fluidly between "work with me" and "go do this for me."

The other big shift in my thinking is how much the environment matters. The model is only as good as what it can see and do. If it can't run your tests, set up your dependencies, or understand how your team works, it'll struggle no matter how smart it is. So a lot of our effort has moved toward giving the agent a good place to work and making its output easy for humans to trust and review. Reviewing code is becoming the bottleneck, so we've put a lot of weight on clear summaries, evidence that things were tested, and small, well-scoped changes.

So, short answer: we started thinking about a tool, and now we think much more about a collaborator that meets you wherever you're working.

r001.rationale: The response describes delegating tasks to the cloud and checking back later, but does not identify continuing work after the user closes their laptop as a reason for initially favoring that form factor.

r002.rationale: It describes the agent as a collaborator available in the developer’s terminal or IDE and summarizes the goal as meeting developers wherever they work.

r003.rationale: It explicitly connects tight-loop local work in a terminal or IDE with asynchronous cloud tasks, describing them as parts of the same agent experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's evolved a lot, and mostly because the models kept changing underneath us.

When we started, the mental model was really autocomplete-plus. You're in the editor, you're typing, and the agent fills in the next few lines or maybe a function. The form factor there is obvious: it lives in the IDE, it's synchronous, you watch it work, and you're the one driving every step. That made sense when the model could only hold a few seconds of coherent intent before it needed a human to correct course.

Then the models got good enough to do a whole task. Not a line, a task. "Fix this bug, write the tests, make CI pass." And the moment that happens, the IDE starts to feel like the wrong container. You don't actually want to sit there and watch a cursor move for twenty minutes. You want to hand it off, go do something else, and come back to a result you can review. So the form factor shifts toward something more like delegation: a terminal, a cloud sandbox, a pull request that shows up in your queue. The unit of interaction becomes the task, not the keystroke.

The part I got wrong early on was thinking this was a one-way migration, that we'd leave the editor behind. It's not. What I believe now is that the right form factor isn't a single surface at all. It's the same agent, with the same understanding of your codebase and your preferences, showing up wherever the work is. Sometimes that's the editor because you're mid-thought and want a quick pair. Sometimes it's the terminal because you want to script it. Sometimes it's a background job that picks up a ticket overnight. The agent is the constant; the surface is a choice.

And then the other big shift is around trust and verification. Once the agent is doing real work unsupervised, the interesting design problem stops being "how do I make the suggestions appear" and becomes "how do I make it easy for a human to verify what happened." Clear diffs, test results you can actually read, the agent explaining what it tried and what it ruled out. A lot of what I think about now is that review surface, because that's the bottleneck. The model can produce more than a person can check, so the form factor has to make checking cheap.

So if I compress it: we went from a tool you drive, to a colleague you delegate to, and the form factor had to follow that. I expect it'll keep moving, and I try to hold my opinions about it a little loosely, because every time the models take a step up, the right shape for the product changes again.

r001.rationale: The response mentions handing off work to a cloud sandbox or background job, but does not identify continuing after the user closes their laptop as a reason for favoring that form factor.

r002.rationale: It describes the same agent appearing in an editor, terminal, or background job, but does not frame bringing the collaborator into developers’ existing tools as the central design goal.

r003.rationale: It combines synchronous editor use with terminal and cloud or background execution, and says the same agent can appear across those surfaces.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve moved away from the idea that there’s one right form factor. When you’re figuring out what to build, you want a very interactive experience. You want to look at the code together, steer the agent, and get quick feedback. But when you have a well-defined task, you want to hand it off and come back to something you can review.

Those are different modes of working, and you can move between them even within a single task. You might start with a conversation, let the agent work independently for a while, and then jump back in when there’s a decision to make.

So the question for me is increasingly: how do we make those transitions feel natural? How does the agent carry the context with it, know when to keep going, and know when it needs your input? I think that matters more than whether the whole experience lives in a terminal, an editor, or a separate app.

r001.rationale: The response describes handing off work and returning later, but does not mention closing a laptop or identify that as the reason for initially favoring a remote asynchronous form factor.

r002.rationale: It says the experience matters more than whether it is in a terminal, editor, or separate app, but does not frame the goal as bringing the agent collaborator into developers’ existing tools.

r003.rationale: It describes moving between interactive and independent work, but does not specify blending cloud asynchronous execution with local synchronous execution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’ve moved from thinking about a coding agent as something that lives in your editor to thinking about it as something you can collaborate with across different environments.

The editor is a very natural starting point. You’re writing code, you have the context right there, and you want help with what you’re doing. But as the agent becomes more capable, you don’t necessarily want to sit there and watch every step. You want to hand it a task, let it work, and come back when there’s something meaningful to review.

So I’m less convinced there’s one right form factor. Sometimes you want a very interactive experience, where you and the agent are working through a problem together. Sometimes you want to delegate something and go do other work. The interesting challenge is making that transition feel natural: giving you visibility and control when you need them, without requiring your attention the whole time.

r001.rationale: The response describes handing off work and returning later, but does not mention working after the user closes their laptop or an initial preference for remote asynchronous execution.

r002.rationale: It says the editor is a natural starting point and mentions different environments, but does not frame the goal as bringing the agent into tools developers already use.

r003.rationale: It contrasts interactive work with delegation, but does not state that cloud asynchronous and local synchronous execution can be blended.
